title: US Immigration Courts Use 'Mega Master' Hearings to Accelerate Deportation Orders
excerpt: Courts are scheduling hearings with 100 or more people at a time, up from the typical two or three dozen, as the Trump administration pushes to deport a million people a year.
body:
• Immigration courts are scheduling 'mega master' hearings with 100 or more respondents at a time, up from the typical 20-30 — a tactic attorneys say is designed to produce more deportation orders.
  • The hearings primarily target immigrants without legal representation; those who arrive late or miss the hearing receive automatic removal orders.
  • Charlotte's immigration court ordered 7,003 removals between January and April 2026 — nearly 86% of all completed cases.
  • A federal appeals court has separately cleared the way for the administration to expand expedited removal to non-citizens apprehended anywhere in the US.

Immigration courts inside the Department of Justice are scheduling mass hearings of 100 or more people at a time — a new and unprecedented tactic that immigration attorneys say is designed to issue deportation orders at a pace the system has never attempted before.

The practice, which immigration lawyers have dubbed "mega masters," was first reported by NPR based on information from the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA). Traditional master calendar hearings — a respondent's first court appearance — typically included two to three dozen people. The new format packs courtrooms far beyond that, with attorneys reporting hearings of well over 100 respondents at a time.

How the System Works

At a master calendar hearing, an immigration judge determines whether a respondent has legal representation, understands the charges against them, and whether the case should proceed to a full hearing. When hearings are scheduled with more than 100 people, the proceedings move faster — but the window for individuals to respond, ask questions, or seek counsel shrinks.

"The major concern is that this is going to be a group of people without attorneys, that they're not going to have gotten proper notice. So it's almost like they are being designed to increase how many people get deportation orders automatically."

— Vanessa Dojaquez-Torres, Practicing Policy Counsel, AILA

Attorneys report that the mega master hearings primarily target immigrants without lawyers. Those who show up late — often because courts lack enough seating — or fail to appear at all are issued in absentia removal orders. AILA said the practice had started in courts in Chicago, Boston, and Chelmsford, Massachusetts, and was expected to expand to Dallas.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), the agency that runs immigration courts within the DOJ, did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

The Numbers

Data from individual courts illustrates the acceleration. Immigration judges at Charlotte's court ordered 7,003 removals between January and April 2026, according to EOIR data — nearly 86 percent of all completed cases during that period. Just 82 cases resulted in immigrants being granted legal relief, about 1 percent of outcomes.

The share of cases ending in removal has climbed steeply: 54 percent in 2024, 72 percent in 2025, and now approaching 86 percent in 2026. Charlotte's court still has a backlog of roughly 129,000 pending cases, the ninth largest in the country.

Expedited Removal Expansion

The court-based acceleration runs parallel to a separate legal victory for the administration. In June, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 to allow the expansion of expedited removal — a fast-track process traditionally used at the border — to cover non-citizens apprehended anywhere in the country who cannot show they have been continuously present for two years.

U.S. Circuit Judge Justin Walker, a Trump appointee, wrote that the administration was allowed to expand "expedited removal to the maximum extent allowed by Congress," overturning a lower court ruling that had blocked the policy on due process grounds.

Impact on the Broader Immigrant Community

The mega master hearings and expanded expedited removal come as the Trump administration pushes toward its stated goal of deporting one million people per year — up from roughly 600,000 deportations in 2025. The combined effect creates a system that processes cases faster but with less opportunity for individuals to present their claims.

For the Indian immigrant community, which includes significant numbers of asylum seekers and those in removal proceedings due to visa overstays, the accelerated pace raises concerns about whether the system provides meaningful due process protections. Immigration courts, unlike criminal courts, do not guarantee the right to a government-provided attorney — making access to legal counsel in these high-volume hearings a critical gap.
nri_angle: The accelerated court proceedings compound fears among documented immigrants, including Indian visa holders, about the broader enforcement climate and due process protections in the US immigration system.
